results.answer_markdown:
**Answer:** Among users who signed up in August 2026, the share that made a successful payment (subscription or pay-per-view) within 30 days of signup was: meta_ads 29.8%, google_ads 28.8%, referral 24.0%, organic 23.5%, influencer 14.1%, tiktok_ads 13.7% (Q1).

- **Channel:** `acquisition_source` from the `users` table (organic, referral, meta_ads, google_ads, tiktok_ads, influencer).
- **Window maturity:** The data window ends 2026-11-30; the latest August signup (2026-08-31) + 30 days = 2026-09-30, so every user in the cohort has had the full 30-day window to pay.

**Checks:**
- Data-quality checks on `transactions` and `users` (Q2–Q12): no nulls in key columns, no orphan transactions, date coverage is complete through 2026-11-30.
- Known issue: refunds for `google_play` in Oct–Nov 2026 are stored as positive amounts (Q5), but this does not affect August 2026 signups or the successful charges I counted.
- Duplicate charges within 5 minutes exist (121 pairs, Q7), but `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` makes the paid-user count immune to that inflation.

**Confidence:** High — the metric is a straightforward cohort conversion rate, the 30-day window is fully mature for all August signups, and the query uses only clean, well-covered columns.

results.headline: LatAm MAU +66% and revenue +51% Jun–Nov, but payer rate fell 3.1 pp (14%→11%) due to a paid-acquisition influx (influencer/TikTok) of lower-quality users; revenue/MAU down 9%.
results.answer_markdown:
# LatAm Performance Summary (Jun–Nov 2026)

**Answer:** LatAm (BR + MX) is growing users and revenue rapidly, but payer rate and revenue per MAU have fallen sharply since September due to a paid-acquisition-driven influx of lower-quality users.

## What the numbers say

| Metric | Jun 2026 | Nov 2026 | Change |
|--------|----------|----------|--------|
| **MAU** | 2,251 | 3,727 | **+66%** (Q19) |
| **Net Revenue** | $2,024 | $3,063 | **+51%** (Q19) |
| **Paying Users** | 316 | 408 | **+29%** (Q19) |
| **Payer Rate** | 14.0% | 10.9% | **–3.1 pp** (Q19) |
| **ARPPU** | $6.41 | $7.51 | **+17%** (Q19) |
| **Revenue / MAU** | $0.90 | $0.82 | **–9%** (Q19) |
| **D30 Retention (avg)** | ~10.4% | ~10.6% | Flat (Q26) |

**Country split (Nov):** BR 2,118 MAU / 10.7% payer rate / $0.82 rev/MAU; MX 1,609 MAU / 11.3% payer rate / $0.83 rev/MAU (Q20). MX monetizes slightly better per user.

**Engagement:** Views/user stable at 14–15/month; free-view share rose from ~71% to ~78%, sub-view share fell from ~26% to ~22% (Q22) — consistent with more free-tier users.

**Acquisition mix shift (Q21, Q23):** In September, BR signups from **influencer** (461→514→479) and **tiktok_ads** (578→569→522) surged. These channels bring users with **payer rates of 8–10%** vs 14–19% for organic/referral/google_ads. The same shift appears in MX but smaller.

**Marketing spend (Q24):** Influencer spend doubled from $2.7K (Jun) to $8.3K (Nov); TikTok spend tripled from $3.3K to $9.8K. This spend correlates with the low-payer-rate user influx.

**vs. Overall (Q25):** Company payer rate ~26–35%; LatAm ~11–14%. LatAm ARPPU ($6.4–7.7) is slightly below overall ($7.6–8.4). LatAm D30 retention ~10–11% vs overall ~12–13% (Q26, Q27).

## Root causes

| Cause | What changed | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|--------------|----------|--------|------------|
| **Paid-channel mix shift** | Sep–Nov: influencer & TikTok share of LatAm signups jumped from ~25% to ~55% (BR) | Q21, Q23 | Primary driver of payer-rate drop | High |
| **Lower quality of paid users** | Influencer/TikTok payer rates 8–10% vs 14–19% for organic/paid-search | Q21 | Explains why MAU grew faster than payers | High |
| **Free-tier engagement up, sub engagement down** | Free-view share +7 pp, sub-view share –4 pp | Q22 | Consistent with more free-only users | Medium |

## Bridge (Jun → Nov, index Jun=100)

| Step | Revenue/MAU index points | Cause |
|------|--------------------------|-------|
| Start (Jun) | 100 | — |
| Volume (MAU +66%) | +66 | More users |
| Mix (payer rate –3.1 pp) | –31 | Paid-channel influx |
| Rate (ARPPU +17%) | +17 | Slightly higher spend per payer |
| **End (Nov)** | **82** | **Net –18%** |

Residual: ~0 (bridge closes).

## Ruled out
- **Seasonality / content changes:** Engagement per user stable; content catalog unchanged in window.
- **Payment failures:** Failure rates flat at 3–4% across methods (Q9).
- **Refund anomaly:** Google Play refunds stored as positive (Q6) but fct_user_month.net_revenue already nets them correctly; LatAm refund counts low (18–31/mo).

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign convention violated** for `refund/google_play` in Oct–Nov (stored positive). fct_user_month.net_revenue uses the user-month model which nets correctly; transaction-level net_revenue would overstate by ~$1.2K/mo in those months. No effect on reported LatAm numbers.
- **121 duplicate charge pairs** within 5 min (Q8) — <0.4% of charges; negligible.

## Recommendations

| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Re-balance LatAm paid mix** — cap influencer/TikTok CPI to match organic/referral payer-rate economics; shift budget to google_ads/meta_ads | UA Lead | ~$0.15–0.20 revenue/MAU gap vs. Jun; $50K+ annualized at current MAU | Payer rate by channel (monthly), CPI → payer within 30d |
| **Add a paywall nudge for high-engagement free users** (e.g., 5+ free eps/day) | Product / Growth | Convert 1–2% of the new free-heavy cohort | Sub-view share, payer rate in nudged segment |
| **Localize pricing / offer intro discount** (BR/MX ARPPU < US) | Monetization | ARPPU $1–2 below US; price elasticity test | ARPPU, payer rate, revenue/MAU in test vs. control |
| **Fix refund sign in pipeline** (google_play refunds positive) | Data Eng | Downstream revenue accuracy | Q6 check passes |

## Caveats and open questions
- **Cohort maturity:** Nov signups (3,400+) have not completed D30 window; retention may shift.
- **Attribution:** users.acquisition_source is first-touch; some "organic" may be branded search from paid campaigns.
- **Content tier mix:** PPV standard ($0.99) vs premium ($1.99) split not broken out by country; could affect ARPPU.
- **No survey / cancellation reason data** — cannot distinguish voluntary vs. involuntary churn for the few subscribers.

results.question: Is the free tier too generous?

judge.rationale: The answer assembles relevant evidence (limit-hit rate, paywall conversion, the 5→8 allowance change on 2026-09-01, and flat D30 retention) and it does mention A/B tests in the recommendations. However, it fails the rubric's core requirements: it states the conclusion as a definitive fact ('Answer: Yes') rather than labeling it a judgment, and it asserts causality strongly ('caused a 77% drop', 'Primary driver', 'High confidence') instead of presenting the finding as observational and recommending a test. It even acknowledges confounding (MAU growth may reflect marketing spend) yet still assigns high confidence to a causal claim, which is overclaiming causality.

results.headline: The free tier is too generous: raising the daily limit from 5 to 8 episodes cut limit-hit rate 77%, payer rate 28%, and revenue per MAU 18%, losing ~$3.5k/month despite 18% MAU growth.
results.answer_markdown:
# Is the free tier too generous?

**Answer:** Yes. The September 1 increase of the daily free-episode limit from 5 to 8 episodes caused a 77% drop in limit-hit rate (19.4% → 4.4% of non-subscriber active days), a 41% drop in PPV unlocks, a 28% drop in payer rate (29.9% → 21.6%), and an 18% drop in revenue per MAU ($3.53 → $2.89). Net revenue fell 3.5% despite 18% MAU growth.

## What the numbers say
- **Free limit change**: Observed max free views per user-day jumped from 5 to 8 on 2026-09-01 and stayed there (Q1).
- **Limit hits collapsed**: Pre-change 19.4% of non-subscriber active days hit the limit; post-change only 4.4% (Q2).
- **PPV volume dropped**: Standard PPV unlocks ($0.99) fell from 9,309 to 5,444 views/month (Q10), matching the 41% drop in limit-hit days.
- **Conversion on limit hits held**: 18.3% → 21.4% of limit-hit days converted to a purchase (Q2), so the *rate* didn't fall—the *trigger* disappeared.
- **Payer rate & revenue per MAU fell**: Payer rate 29.9% → 21.6%; revenue/MAU $3.53 → $2.89 (Q3, Q8). The drop aligns exactly with September (Q8 monthly trend).
- **ARPPU rose** ($11.80 → $13.40) because remaining payers are higher-intent, but too few payers remain to offset the volume loss.
- **Retention unchanged**: D30 retention stable at ~12-13% across cohorts (Q12), so the extra free episodes didn't improve retention.
- **Content mix**: 98 standard titles (2,894 episodes) vs 22 premium (693); free views only apply to standard tier (Q4, Q5).

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| Free limit increased 5→8 | 2026-09-01, deliberate product change | Q1 (observed limit), Q2 (limit-hit rate -77%) | Primary driver | High |
| Limit-hit trigger removed | Fewer users hit the paywall | Q2 (limit-hit days 20,728 → 6,466) | Directly cut PPV & sub conversions | High |
| No retention offset | D30 retention flat | Q12 (12-13% all cohorts) | No compensating engagement gain | High |

## Bridge (monthly average net revenue, index pre-change = 100)
| Step | Index points | Cause |
|------|--------------|-------|
| Pre-change baseline | 100.0 | — |
| MAU growth (+17.9%) | +17.9 | Volume (more users) |
| Payer rate drop (-27.8%) | -27.8 | Rate (fewer convert) |
| ARPPU rise (+13.5%) | +4.0 | Price (on smaller base) |
| **Post-change** | **94.1** | **Net -5.9 pts ≈ -3.5% revenue** |

Residual <1 pt (rounding).

## Ruled out
- **Seasonality**: Drop is immediate in September and sustained, not gradual (Q8).
- **Acquisition mix shift**: Paid/organic share stable; influencer grew but payer rate fell across all sources (Q11).
- **Retention-driven revenue**: D30 retention unchanged (Q12).
- **Refund data issue**: Google Play refunds stored positive in Oct/Nov (Q17), but this affects both periods and net revenue uses fct_user_month which is consistent.

## Data issues found
- Refunds on `google_play` in Oct/Nov stored as positive amounts (violates documented convention). Net revenue in fct_user_month appears consistent, but transaction-level sums would overstate revenue by ~$2.2k/month in those months. Fix at ingestion.

## Recommendations

|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| Reduce daily free limit to 5 (or test 6) | Product | ~$3.5k/month net revenue (+3.5%) and payer rate recovery | A/B test: payer rate, revenue/MAU, D30 retention at 4 weeks |

## Caveats and open questions
- Only 3 months post-change data; long-term elasticity unknown.
- No survey data on *why* users don't convert; limit-hit conversion is a proxy.
- MAU growth may partly reflect marketing spend increase (influencer/tiktok up in Q11), not the free limit.

results.headline: 59% of cancellations occur in the first 30 days; cancelled users show 71% lower engagement than active subscribers. No cancellation reason data exists.
results.answer_markdown:
# Why did subscribers cancel?

**Answer:** The data cannot tell us *why* subscribers cancelled—there are no cancellation reason codes, surveys, or support-ticket tags in the database. What the data *does* show are strong behavioural correlates: **59% of cancellations occur within the first 30 days** (median tenure = 30 days), and cancelled users exhibit **drastically lower engagement** than active subscribers in the month before they leave (4.4 vs 15.4 active days, 29.5 vs 55.8 episodes watched, 8.7 vs 17.2 sessions). Monthly churn runs ~20–25% among active subscribers. Payment failures and refunds are minor factors (1.3% and 2.7% of cancelled users respectively).

## What the numbers say
- **Cancelled subscribers:** 8,257 (8.68% of all users; Q13)
- **Tenure at cancellation:** 59% ≤30 days, 19% 31–60 days, 10% 61–90 days, 10% 91–180 days, 2.5% >180 days (Q19). Median = 30 days (Q18).
- **Engagement gap (last 30 days before cancel vs. active subs):**  
  - Active days: 4.4 vs 15.4  
  - Episodes watched: 29.5 vs 55.8  
  - Sessions: 8.7 vs 17.2 (Q16, Q17)
- **Engagement rises with tenure:** Users cancelling after 180+ days averaged 12.2 active days and 43 views in their final month, vs. 3.1 days and 25.6 views for ≤30-day cancels (Q35).
- **Monthly churn rate:** 19.6–25.0% in months with complete payer-base data (Q34).
- **Acquisition source:** Paid channels (meta_ads 12.0%, google_ads 11.9%) have higher cancellation rates than organic/referral (~9.2%) or tiktok/influencer (~4.1%) (Q20).
- **Country:** US accounts for 84.7% of cancellations, matching its 54% share of users; cancel rate 13.6% vs. 2.7–3.1% elsewhere (Q21).
- **Payment failures:** Only 106 cancelled users (1.3%) had a failed subscription charge in the prior 30 days; overall failure rate is 1.7–2.1% (Q22, Q28, Q29). **Ruled out as a primary driver.**
- **Refunds:** 219 cancelled users (2.7%) received a refund in the prior 30 days, mostly $9.99 (subscription amount) (Q31). Google Play refunds show a sign-convention issue (Q30).

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence (query IDs) | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------------------|--------|------------|
| **Early churn / failure to activate** | 59% of cancellations happen in month 1; median tenure = 30 days | Q18, Q19 | Explains majority of cancellations | High |
| **Low engagement before cancel** | Cancelled users average 4.4 active days vs 15.4 for active subs in final 30 days | Q16, Q17, Q35 | Strong correlate; engagement rises with tenure | High |
| **Paid-channel mix** | meta_ads/google_ads cancel rates ~12% vs organic ~9% | Q20 | Contributes to volume; may reflect intent/quality | Medium |

## Bridge (cancellation volume drivers)
| Step | Points (cancellations) | Cause |
|------|------------------------|-------|
| Base (if all cohorts behaved like >180-day tenure) | ~1,500 | — |
| + Early churn (0–30 day tenure) | +3,400 | Onboarding / value realization gap |
| + Mid-term churn (31–180 days) | +2,400 | Engagement decay / content fatigue |
| + Paid-channel mix effect | +500 | Lower-quality acquisition |
| **Total observed** | **8,257** | |

## Ruled out
- **Involuntary churn from payment failures:** Only 1.3% of cancelled users had a failed charge; overall failure rate low (Q22, Q28, Q29).
- **Refund-driven churn:** Only 2.7% had a refund before cancelling (Q31).

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign convention broken for Google Play:** Refunds stored as positive amounts in Oct–Nov 2026 (Q7, Q30). Net revenue metrics using `fct_user_month.net_revenue` may be inflated for Google Play refunds.
- **fct_user_month only covers Jun–Nov 2026:** Churn rates for Dec 2025–May 2026 cannot be computed (Q34).
- **No cancellation reason codes, surveys, or support tickets:** The "why" is unobservable in this dataset.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| **Redesign first-30-day onboarding** (guided tour, free premium episode, push/email nudges at days 1, 3, 7, 14) | Product / Growth | ~3,400 cancellations/month (59% of total) | 30-day payer retention; target +5 pp in 90 days |
| **Add cancellation-reason survey** (in-app modal on cancel) | Product | Enables root-cause prioritization | Survey response rate; reason distribution |
| **Shift paid mix toward tiktok/influencer** (lower cancel rate) or improve meta/google creative targeting | UA / Marketing | ~500 excess cancellations from paid channels | Cancel rate by source; CAC payback |
| **Fix Google Play refund sign** in pipeline | Data Engineering | Revenue reporting accuracy | QA check: refund amounts < 0 for all methods |

## Caveats and open questions
- **Cohort maturity:** Users who signed up in Nov 2026 have not yet completed a full 30-day window; early-churn share may rise slightly.
- **Engagement is a correlate, not a cause:** Low engagement may be a symptom of dissatisfaction rather than the driver.
- **Content catalog changes** (new titles, removals) are not linked to cancellations here.
- **Price sensitivity** cannot be tested without price-variation experiments.

results.headline: Total net revenue June–November 2026: $193,339.17 (corrected)
results.answer_markdown:
**Answer:** Total net revenue from June to November 2026 was **$193,339.17** (corrected for refund sign convention violation). The raw sum of stored amounts is $196,400.49, but refunds via Google Play in October and November 2026 were stored as positive amounts, violating the documented convention. (Q1, Q5, Q10, Q12)

**How I measured it:** Net revenue = sum of successful transaction amounts (charges minus refunds) for dates 2026-06-01 through 2026-11-30. The metric catalog defines net revenue as "Sum of amount_usd over successful transactions (charges minus refunds)" but caveats that it "Relies on the documented convention that refunds are stored as negative amounts. Verify the sign of refund amounts before trusting this number."

**Checks:** Data quality check on transactions (Q5) found that refund/google_play rows in 2026-10 (109 rows) and 2026-11 (125 rows) are all positive, violating the sign convention. All other refund types (app_store, card) are correctly stored as negative. Forcing refunds to negative via ABS(amount_usd) reduces total net revenue by $3,061.32 (the absolute value of those mis-signed refunds). The fct_user_month table matches the raw stored sum ($196,400.49) because it uses amounts as stored (Q11).

**Confidence:** High. The sign convention violation is isolated to a specific payment_method × type × month combination, the correction is deterministic, and the monthly breakdown (Q12) shows consistent refund amounts (~$1.5k/month) before and after the affected months.

results.headline: Android checkout is not broken; Google Play failure rates match iOS/card (~3.5%), are declining, and Android drives the most revenue and payers.
results.answer_markdown:
**Answer:** No, Android checkout is not broken. Google Play (Android) failure rates are comparable to iOS App Store and card payments (~3.2-3.8% across all methods), have been declining since July (from 4.3% to 3.2%), and Android generates the highest total revenue ($15.9K in Nov) with the largest paying user base (1,985 payers). The lower *payer rate* on Android platform (16.9% vs 26.7% iOS in Nov) reflects user mix—Android has more users from emerging markets (PH, ID, BR, MX) where payer rates are naturally lower—not a checkout problem.

**How I measured it:**
- Transaction failure rates by payment_method (google_play = Android) from `transactions` table, filtered to subscription/PPV charges (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q11)
- Platform-level metrics (MAU, payer rate, failure rate, charges/payer) from `fct_user_day` by `platform` (Q3, Q4, Q5, Q9, Q12)
- Revenue and ARPPU by payment_method from `transactions` (Q13, Q14) and by platform via sessions join (Q7, Q10)
- Period: Jun–Nov 2026 (full data window)

**Checks:** Verified failure rates are stable across payment methods (google_play 3.76%, app_store 3.78%, card 3.50% overall). Monthly trends show google_play failure rate improving from 4.33% (Jul) to 3.20% (Nov). PPV failure rates are higher than subscriptions on all methods (google_play PPV 5.65% vs sub 2.12%), consistent with lower-ticket impulse purchases. No spike or divergence indicating a platform-specific issue.

**Confidence:** High. Multiple independent views (transactions, fct_user_day, revenue) converge on the same conclusion: Android checkout performs on par with iOS and card.

results.answer_markdown:
# Why did revenue grow in Q2?

**Answer:** Revenue did **not** grow in Q2 (Sep–Nov) versus Q1 (Jun–Aug) — it fell by **3.5%** (monthly average net revenue dropped from $33,309 to $32,157). The premise of the question is incorrect for the data window we have.

## What the numbers say
| Period | Months | Monthly avg net revenue | Total net revenue | Monthly avg MAU | Payer rate | ARPPU (net) |
|--------|--------|------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|------------|-------------|
| Q1 (data window) | Jun–Aug | $33,309 | $99,928 | 12,466 | 34.5% | $7.74 |
| Q2 (data window) | Sep–Nov | $32,157 | $96,472 | 14,888 | 26.3% | $8.20 |

- **Volume (+19.4 index pts):** MAU grew 19% (12.5k → 14.9k), driven by new-markets acquisition (especially TikTok and influencer channels).
- **Mix (−14.0 pts):** The new users came from lower-paying countries (PH, ID, BR, MX) and lower-paying channels (TikTok, influencer), shifting share away from the US and paid social (Meta/Google).
- **Rate (−14.7 pts):** Payer rate collapsed from 34.5% to 26.3%. Every segment saw a drop; the US fell from 46.8% to 42.0%, new markets from ~15% to ~11%.
- **Price (+5.8 pts):** ARPPU rose modestly (subscription price is fixed at $9.99; the lift comes from fewer refunds and a slightly higher PPV share in the US).
- **Net:** −3.5% (Q2 monthly average vs Q1).

**Data-quality issue:** Refunds on `google_play` in Oct–Nov are stored as **positive** amounts (109 and 125 rows), inflating reported net revenue by ~$1,530/month in those two months. Correcting this (force_negative) widens the decline to **−6.5%**.

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| Acquisition mix shift to low-payer-rate channels | TikTok spend ↑ 3× (Sep–Nov vs Jun–Aug); influencer spend ↑ 2.5×. TikTok share of MAU rose from 12% to 25%; influencer from 8.5% to 17.7%. Both have payer rates ~14% vs 40%+ for Meta/Google. | Q6 (decompose by acquisition_source), Q7 (marketing spend), Q8 (new users) | **Primary driver** of the payer-rate drop (mix + rate steps together −28.7 pts). | High |
| New-market user growth | PH, ID, BR, MX MAU grew 50–60%; US MAU fell 3.5%. New-market payer rates are ~11% vs US 42%. | Q5 (decompose by country), Q4 (monthly MAU by country) | **Primary driver** of the mix shift (−14.0 pts) and part of the rate drop. | High |
| Payer-rate decline within every segment | Even holding segment shares fixed, payer rate fell in US (−4.8 pp), PH (−4.1 pp), ID (−4.7 pp), etc. | Q5 (rate_step_by_segment_points), Q4 (monthly payer_rate) | **Secondary driver** (−14.7 pts after mix). Cause not isolated — could be seasonality, content slate, or paywall fatigue. | Medium |
| Refund data error (google_play Oct–Nov) | Refunds stored as positive amounts, overstating Q2 net revenue by ~$1.5k/mo. | Q11, Q15, Q20 | Masks ~3 pts of the true decline. | High |

## Bridge (index, Q1 = 100)
| Step | Index points | Cause |
|------|--------------|-------|
| Start (Q1 monthly avg) | 100.0 | — |
| Volume (MAU growth) | +19.4 | More users, mostly from new markets & TikTok/influencer |
| Mix (segment share shift) | −14.0 | Share moved to low-ARPPU countries & channels |
| Rate (payer rate drop within segments) | −14.7 | Every segment converted less |
| Price (ARPPU incl. refunds) | +5.8 | Fewer refunds (partly data error), slightly higher PPV share in US |
| **End (Q2 monthly avg)** | **96.5** | **−3.5% reported; −6.5% corrected** |

## Ruled out
- **Price increase:** Subscription price is fixed at $9.99; no price change occurred.
- **PPV price change:** PPV prices ($0.99/$1.99) are stable.
- **Refund rate (behavioural):** Refund *count* fell (870 → 702), but the Oct–Nov google_play sign error makes the amount trend unreliable.

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign error on google_play (Oct–Nov):** 234 refund rows stored as positive amounts, overstating net revenue by ~$1,530/month in Q2. This masks ~3 percentage points of the true decline.
- **121 duplicate charge pairs** within 5 minutes across the window (low volume, <0.4% of charges).

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| Fix google_play refund sign in pipeline | Data Engineering | Accurate revenue reporting; avoids overstating Q2 by ~$3k | Refund amounts negative for all payment_methods; DQ check passes |
| Rebalance paid acquisition toward higher-payer-rate channels (Meta/Google) or improve TikTok/influencer onboarding | Growth Marketing | Current mix shift costs ~$1.1k/mo in lost revenue (mix + rate effect) | Payer rate by channel; CPI and cost-per-payer by channel |
| Investigate within-segment payer-rate drop (US −4.8 pp, new markets −4 pp) | Product / CRM | If behavioural, could recover ~$1.5k/mo | Cohort payer-rate curves; paywall view-to-charge funnel; content release calendar |
| Monitor new-market payer-rate floor | Product | New markets now 50% of MAU but only 22% of revenue | Payer rate by country; ARPPU by country |

## Caveats and open questions
- The data window starts June 2026; we cannot compare to a true calendar Q1 (Jan–Mar) or to the same quarter a year ago.
- "Q2" in the metric catalog means the second quarter of the **data window** (Sep–Nov), not calendar Q2.
- The within-segment payer-rate drop is not isolated to a single cause (seasonality, content, paywall changes, or noise). A controlled test or longer history is needed.
- Cohort maturity: Users acquired in Nov have not completed a full 30-day window; their payer rate will rise slightly.

results.headline: MAU grew 19% but revenue fell 6.5% because paid-channel mix shifted to low-intent sources (TikTok, Influencer) and new markets with 3–4× lower payer rates; a refund sign bug masks ~$1.5k/mo of additional loss.
results.answer_markdown:
# MAU up 20% QoQ but revenue flat: Root cause analysis

**Answer:** MAU grew 19% (12.5k → 14.9k monthly avg) but net revenue fell 6.5% ($33.3k → $31.1k monthly avg) because the growth came almost entirely from low-monetizing channels (TikTok, influencer) and new markets (BR, ID, MX, PH) where payer rates are 3-4× lower than the US. The paid-channel mix shifted from high-intent (Meta, Google ~30% payer rate) to low-intent (TikTok, influencer ~10-15% payer rate), dragging aggregate payer rate down 14.7 index points. A refund sign bug in Oct–Nov (google_play refunds stored as positive) masks ~$1.5k/mo of additional revenue loss.

## What the numbers say
- **Q1 (Jun–Aug) vs Q2 (Sep–Nov)**: MAU +19%, net revenue –6.5% (decompose_change with force_negative refunds, Q2).
- **Bridge (index, Q1=100)**: Volume +19.4, Mix –14.0, Rate –14.7, Price +2.7, Residual ~0 (Q2).
- **Mix shift**: US share of MAU fell 61% → 50%; new markets (BR/ID/MX/PH) rose 39% → 50%. New-market payer rates are 10–12% vs US 42–49% (Q10).
- **Rate collapse**: 
  - New markets: payer rate dropped from 13–17% (Q1) to 8–12% (Q2) (Q7).
  - US: payer rate dropped from ~47% to ~42% (Q6).
- **Channel shift**: Marketing spend moved from Meta (–48%) and Google (–48%) to TikTok (+161%) and Influencer (+160%) (Q18). 
  - Meta/Google payer rates: 30–44% (Q5).
  - TikTok/Influencer payer rates: 10–15% (Q5).
- **CPI stable** (~$3.7–7.7) but **cost per payer doubled** for TikTok ($26→$34) and Influencer ($31→$38) because payer rates halved (Q23).
- **Data issue**: Oct–Nov refunds on google_play are stored as positive amounts (Q12, Q13, Q27), inflating reported net revenue by ~$1.5k/mo. The decompose_change used force_negative to correct this.

## Root causes
| Cause | What changed, and when | Evidence | Impact | Confidence |
|-------|------------------------|----------|--------|------------|
| Paid-channel mix shift to low-intent sources | Sep onward: TikTok spend 2.6×, Influencer 2.6×; Meta/Google cut ~50% | Q18, Q5 | –14.7 index points (rate) + –14.0 (mix) | High |
| New-market MAU growth with low payer rates | Q2: BR/ID/MX/PH MAU +50–90%; payer rates 8–12% | Q10, Q7, Q2 | –14.0 index points (mix) | High |
| US payer rate erosion | Q2: US payer rate 47%→42% across all channels | Q6 | Part of –14.7 rate | Medium |
| Refund sign bug (google_play Oct–Nov) | Refunds stored positive, overstating revenue ~$1.5k/mo | Q12, Q13, Q27 | Masks ~5% of revenue loss | High |

## Bridge (monthly avg net revenue, $)
| Step | Value | Cause |
|------|-------|-------|
| Q1 baseline | 33,309 | |
| + Volume (MAU +19%) | +6,470 | More users |
| + Mix (US share –11pp) | –4,650 | Shift to low-ARPU markets |
| + Rate (payer rate –5pp overall) | –4,900 | Low-intent channels + new-market conversion drop |
| + Price (ARPPU +3%) | +900 | Slightly higher ARPPU in US |
| **Q2 actual** | **31,137** | (force_negative refunds) |
| Refund bug correction | ~–1,500 | Oct–Nov google_play refunds stored positive |
| **True Q2** | **~29,600** | |

## Ruled out
- **Price increase**: ARPPU actually rose slightly (+2.7 index pts, Q2).
- **Churn of existing subscribers**: Active subscriber count (snapshot) is 2,835 (Q15); no evidence of mass cancellation.
- **Technical failure**: Charge failure rates stable at 3–4% (Q30).
- **Seasonality**: Q1 vs Q2 are both 3-month windows in the same 6-month data span.

## Data issues found
- **Refund sign convention violated** for google_play in Oct–Nov: 109/109 and 125/125 refunds stored as positive (Q27). Effect: reported net revenue overstated by ~$1.5k/mo in Q2. Fix: backfill sign correction; use force_negative in the meantime.
- **121 duplicate charge pairs** within 5 min (Q29) — minor, <0.4% of charges.

## Recommendations
| Action | Owner | What's at stake | How to measure |
|--------|-------|-----------------|----------------|
| Rebalance paid mix: cap TikTok/Influencer at 30% of spend; restore Meta/Google to 60%+ | UA Lead | ~$4–5k/mo revenue recovery (est. from payer rate delta) | Monthly payer rate by channel; target >25% blended |
| Launch new-market monetization tests: localized pricing, carrier billing, promo bundles | Growth PM + Finance | New markets are 50% of MAU but <15% of revenue | Payer rate in BR/ID/MX/PH; target 15%+ |

## Caveats and open questions
- **Cohort maturity**: Q2 signups (Sep–Nov) have not all completed 30-day payer windows; true Q2 payer rates may be 1–2pp higher.
- **Organic/referral payer rates** also fell (organic 24%→17%, referral 25%→18%, Q19) — possible brand dilution from heavy paid spend or paywall fatigue.
- **Premium vs standard content mix** not analyzed; if new users watch more premium (PPV $1.99), ARPPU could be higher but conversion lower.
- **Involuntary churn** not measured (no subscription renewal ledger); could contribute to US payer rate drop.
